title: Longest Palindromic Substring — expand-around-center O(n²) or Manacher's O(n).
shortTitle: Longest Palindromic Substring — Expand Around Center O(n²)

s1_definition.profdef: The Longest Palindromic Substring problem finds the longest contiguous substring that reads the same forward and backward. The expand-around-center solution treats every position, and every gap between positions, as a potential palindrome center and expands outward while the mirrored characters match, keeping the longest span found. It runs in quadratic time with constant extra space, while Manacher's algorithm achieves linear time with more complex bookkeeping.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India scans a reference string and wants the longest stretch that is symmetric like a mirror. The idea is to stand at every possible center, both on a character and between two characters, and push outward one step at a time as long as the characters on the left and right keep matching. Whichever center produces the widest mirror wins. It is like dropping a pin at each spot and seeing how far the symmetry extends.
s1_definition.oneliner: Try every character and every gap as a center, expand while both sides match, and keep the longest.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The Longest Palindromic Substring problem finds the longest contiguous substring that reads the same forward and backward. The expand-around-center solution treats every position, and every gap between positions, as a potential palindrome center and expands outward while the mirrored characters match, keeping the longest span found. It runs in quadratic time with constant extra space, while Manacher's algorithm achieves linear time with more complex bookkeeping.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India scans a reference string and wants the longest stretch that is symmetric like a mirror. The idea is to stand at every possible center, both on a character and between two characters, and push outward one step at a time as long as the characters on the left and right keep matching. Whichever center produces the widest mirror wins. It is like dropping a pin at each spot and seeing how far the symmetry extends.

**One line to remember:** Try every character and every gap as a center, expand while both sides match, and keep the longest.

sections.s2_technical:
A palindrome is defined by a center and symmetric expansion. There are two kinds of centers: an odd-length palindrome has a single character at its center, and an even-length palindrome has its center between two characters. So for a string of length n there are 2n minus one possible centers, one at each character and one in each gap between adjacent characters.

The expand-around-center method loops over every index and treats it both as an odd center, with left and right both starting at that index, and as an even center, with left at that index and right at the next index. For each center you expand: while the left index is in bounds, the right index is in bounds, and the characters at left and right are equal, you move left one step back and right one step forward. When the expansion stops, the palindrome spans from just inside the final left to just inside the final right, and you compute its length. You track the overall longest span, remembering its start and end to return the substring at the end.

The time is quadratic because there are a linear number of centers and each expansion can take linear time in the worst case, such as a string of all identical characters. The space is constant because you only track indices and the best span, never building extra structures. This quadratic approach is the one most interviewers expect you to code correctly, with Manacher's linear algorithm as a known follow-up rather than the default.

A senior point is handling both center parities in one pass with a small helper. The helper takes a left and right starting index and returns the length of the palindrome centered there after expanding. You call it once with left equal to right for odd centers and once with right equal to left plus one for even centers, take the larger, and if it beats the best, update the start and end using arithmetic on the center and the returned length. Getting the start and end arithmetic exactly right, especially the even case, is where bugs hide.

Another senior point is Manacher's algorithm, which reaches linear time by transforming the string with separators and reusing previously computed palindrome radii via a mirror property around the current rightmost palindrome boundary. I mention that it exists and is linear, but I note it is rarely required to code live and is error-prone, so I lead with expand-around-center and offer Manacher's as the optimization if pressed.

A small finance-domain example: `for(int i=0;i<n;i++){ int a=expand(s,i,i); int b=expand(s,i,i+1); int len=Math.max(a,b); if(len>best){ start=i-(len-1)/2; end=i+len/2; } }` finds the longest mirrored span.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India examines reference strings for the longest symmetric segment, a mirror-like run, as part of a pattern-detection utility that flags unusual structured identifiers. The strings are moderate in length, so the quadratic expand-around-center approach is acceptable and simplest to get right. Finding the longest palindromic substring is exactly this.

This is exactly how expand-around-center works in Java — trying every character and every gap as a center and expanding while both sides match.

Problem 2 — Palindromes can be odd length, centered on a character, or even length, centered between two characters, and both must be checked, and an empty or single-character string is trivially its own answer. This shows the two-parity centers and the trivial edge cases.

What the code will do: a `PalindromeFinder` with `longestPalindrome(String s)` using expand-around-center over both parities, tracking the best span. The demo finds the longest palindromic substring in several reference strings.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: the reference string `babad`.

Step 1: at index zero, character `b`, the odd expansion starts with left and right both zero. The characters match trivially, then left goes to minus one which is out of bounds, so expansion stops with length one. The even expansion with left zero and right one compares `b` and `a`, which differ, so length zero. The best length so far is one, span is just `b`.

Step 2: at index one, character `a`, the odd expansion compares outward: left zero `b` and right two `b` match, so it expands to the substring `bab` of length three, then left minus one stops it. The even expansion compares `a` and `b`, differ, length zero. Three beats one, so we update the span: start is index one minus one which is zero, end is index one plus one which is two, giving `bab`.

Step 3: at index two, character `b`, the odd expansion compares left one `a` and right three `a`, match, expanding to `aba` of length three, then left zero `b` and right four `d` differ, stopping. Length three ties the best but does not exceed it, so the span stays `bab`.

Step 4: at indices three and four the expansions produce lengths of at most one, not beating three. The loop ends with the span `bab`, which we return. Depending on tie handling, `aba` is an equally valid answer; this implementation keeps the first longest found.

Step 5: for `cbbd` the even center between the two `b` characters at indices one and two expands to `bb` of length two, which beats the odd single-character palindromes, so the answer is `bb`. For a single character `a` the odd expansion gives length one and the answer is `a`.

Final output:

```
2026-10-26T21:20:00Z INFO Longest palindrome = 'bab'
2026-10-26T21:20:00Z INFO Result = bab
2026-10-26T21:20:00Z INFO Longest palindrome = 'bb'
2026-10-26T21:20:00Z INFO Result = bb
2026-10-26T21:20:00Z INFO Longest palindrome = 'a'
2026-10-26T21:20:00Z INFO Result = a
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: "babad"
    │ for each center i: expand odd (i,i) and even (i,i+1)
    ▼
  i0 'b' odd→1 ; i1 'a' odd→3 ("bab") update span [0..2]
  i2 'b' odd→3 ("aba") ties, no update ; i3,i4 → <=1
    │ best span [0..2]
    ▼
  substring(0,3) = "bab"   ("cbbd"→even center→"bb")
    ▼
  Output: longest palindromic substring
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Longest Palindromic Substring finds the longest contiguous substring that reads the same both ways, and I solve it with expand-around-center in quadratic time and constant space. The insight is that every palindrome has a center, and there are two kinds: an odd-length palindrome centered on a single character and an even-length one centered between two characters, giving two times n minus one possible centers for a string of length n.

For each index I expand twice, once as an odd center with left and right both at the index, and once as an even center with right one past left, pushing outward while the characters on both sides match and stay in bounds. A small helper returns the palindrome length for a given center, and I use the center and that length to compute the start and end of the span, keeping the longest. Getting the start and end arithmetic right, especially for the even case, is where most bugs appear, so I derive it carefully.

I always mention Manacher's algorithm as the linear-time follow-up. It transforms the string with separators and reuses previously computed palindrome radii through a mirror property around the current rightmost palindrome, reaching linear time, but it is intricate and error-prone to write live, so I lead with expand-around-center and offer Manacher's only if asked for better than quadratic. I also handle the trivial cases where an empty or single-character string is its own answer.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used expand-around-center in a pattern-detection utility that flags reference strings containing an unusually long symmetric segment, checking both odd and even centers over moderate-length identifiers. Explaining the two center parities, the expansion helper, the span arithmetic, and knowing when Manacher's would be warranted shows the interviewer that I can implement the expected solution correctly while being aware of the optimal one.
